exercises.instructions:
Create a Query that returns a product. Use #[SimpleObject].

📚 https://async-graphql.github.io/async-graphql/en/define_simple_object.html

Make the test ex01 pass!

Add another Simple object (Order) and a custom resolver for OrderLine. Use #[ComplexObject].

📚 https://async-graphql.github.io/async-graphql/en/define_simple_object.html#user-defined-resolvers

Make the test ex02 pass!

We want split the 2 bounded contexts. 

Expose both product and order queries using #[MergedObject].

📚 https://async-graphql.github.io/async-graphql/en/merging_objects.html

Make the test ex03 pass!

Enrich the domain model:

Add a status field as an Enum to Order.

Add a Customer field (SimpleObject with id/name/vat).

Add a price field to order lines. It is a scalar type (amount + currency), and also a discount field of the same money type, but optional.

📚 https://async-graphql.github.io/async-graphql/en/define_enum.html
📚 https://async-graphql.github.io/async-graphql/en/custom_scalars.html

Make the ex04 test pass!

Change the Product type to return a Union of Products: 

Standard Product

DangerousProduct (with maxTemperature)

ExpiringProduct (with expirationDate).

📚 https://async-graphql.github.io/async-graphql/en/define_union.html

Make the test ex05 pass!

There is a lot of duplication into the query.

Put the common fields (id, code, description) into an Interface.

📚 https://async-graphql.github.io/async-graphql/en/define_interface.html

Make the test ex06 pass!

Let's create a new product.

Add a createProduct mutation using #[InputObject].

Persist the product to the database and return the created Product. 
All the db statements are into the db folder.

Refactor the whole schema to remove the struct creation and replace it with the database operations.

📚 https://async-graphql.github.io/async-graphql/en/define_input_object.html

Make the test ex07 pass!

Change the mutation input to be a #[OneofObject] (CreateProductKind).

Accepting one of: product, dangerousProduct, or expiringProduct.

📚 https://async-graphql.github.io/async-graphql/en/define_one_of_object.html

Make the test ex08 pass!

Split into two federated subgraphs: products (port 3001) and orders (port 3002).

Orders references ProductKind via @interfaceObject. 

Use `cargo make local` to run with the router on port 5000.

📚 https://async-graphql.github.io/async-graphql/en/apollo_federation.html

Make the test ex09 pass!

Add a customers subgraph (port 3003) behind a feature flag that overrides the customer name from the orders subgraph using @override. 

Follow the federation part of the cargo make help.

📚 https://async-graphql.github.io/async-graphql/en/apollo_federation.html

Make the test ex10 pass!

Use DataLoader to batch Product queries.

You have an Order with multiple OrderLines, each referencing a Product.

Without DataLoader, OrderLine.product resolver is called N times → N database queries (N+1 problem).

Implement a DataLoader<ProductId, Product> that batches the product IDs and loads them in a single query.

The Product resolver (get_product_details) simulates a DB call that should only happen once per batch of unique product IDs.

📚 https: //async-graphql.github.io/async-graphql/en/data_loader.html

Make the test ex11 pass!

Apply DataLoader to the federated architecture (ex09).

Without DataLoader, the products subgraph receives one _entities call from the router with 50 representations, but invokes find_product_by_id 50 times sequentially → 50 DB queries.

Implement a DataLoader inside the products subgraph to batch these calls → 1-2 DB queries.

The key insight: federation's network batching ≠ database batching. You need DataLoader inside each subgraph.

📚 https: //async-graphql.github.io/async-graphql/en/data_loader.html

Make the test ex12 pass!
